nameStory: The Sharp Sprite gets its mystical name from its delicate, almost ethereal appearance - like a tiny water spirit gliding through quiet ponds. The 'sharp' part refers to the pointed spire of its shell, which distinguishes it from its flatter ramshorn relatives.
description: The Sharp Sprite is a tiny freshwater snail that belongs to the ramshorn snail family, though it looks quite different from the flat, coiled shells most people associate with ramshorns. Instead of a pancake-flat spiral, this little mollusk sports a more pointed, cone-like shell that spirals upward. These miniature aquatic snails are extremely rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery. They're small enough that you'd need to look carefully to spot one gliding along submerged plants or the muddy bottom of a quiet water body.

idTips.label: Pointed spire shape
idTips.description: Unlike typical flat ramshorn snails, the shell rises to a distinct point, feeling almost cone-like when gently touched

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Extremely small, easily fitting on a fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Translucent shell
idTips.description: Shell appears somewhat see-through with a glassy, smooth texture when held up to light

idTips.label: Spiral pattern
idTips.description: Shell coils in a tight spiral that you can trace with your finger, but rises upward rather than staying flat

idTips.label: Aquatic movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along underwater surfaces, leaving a barely visible slime trail

habitat: Sharp Sprites inhabit quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow-moving streams, and marshes with soft, muddy bottoms rich in organic matter. They prefer areas with abundant aquatic vegetation where they can graze on algae and decomposing plant material. Look for them in shallow, protected areas where the water moves gently and sediment can accumulate.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, often found grazing on early algae growth on submerged surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be spotted moving along pond bottoms and plant stems.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to deeper areas as surface waters begin to cool.
seasonality.winter: Dormant in bottom sediments, essentially impossible to find without disturbing substrate.

funFact: With only 2 recorded observations in all of New England, finding a Sharp Sprite is rarer than spotting many endangered birds - you'd literally be among the first handful of people to document this tiny snail in our region!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young pond snails, but remember the Sharp Sprite's shell spirals upward in a pointed cone while pond snails have more rounded, bulbous shells. The pointed spire that gives this species its name is your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'ramshorn' snail, Sharp Sprites don't look like the typical flat, disk-shaped ramshorns most people know. This family is more diverse than many realize, with some species developing tall spires instead of flat coils.
compareHints: Since no other Promenetus species are found in New England, compare the Sharp Sprite to other small freshwater snails in the ramshorn family. Unlike typical ramshorns with their characteristic flat, coiled shells that lie horizontal, the Sharp Sprite's shell rises vertically in a pointed spire. This makes it look more like a tiny pond snail at first glance, but the spiral pattern and family characteristics set it apart.
